item.title: Death on the Night Mail: An Easy Murder Mystery Logic Grid
item.description:
Clue five says Mr. Quill was two compartments nearer the engine than Miss Ingram. You count it out on your fingers: Compartments 1 and 3, or 2 and 4. That’s it. Two possibilities. Then you reread clue one, and one of them quietly falls off the train.

This is the smallest kind of logic grid: four passengers, four compartments, four pieces of luggage, and only five clues. Each passenger had exactly one compartment and carried exactly one thing. The clues are all true, and they’re enough to place everyone without a single guess. If you’ve never solved a logic grid before, start here.

item.title: Death at Ravenscroft Manor: A Murder Mystery Logic Grid
item.description:
You have nine clues and a dead lord. Clue one says Dr. Pryce wasn’t seen at 9:45. Fine. Clue three says he wasn’t seen at 9:30 either. Two ✕s later, the doctor’s row in the Time block has only two squares left, and clue eight is already whispering about which one. That narrowing is the reason people have been doing these on train rides for sixty years.

This one is a classic logic grid: every guest was in exactly one room, holding exactly one object, at exactly one time. Nothing is shared and nothing is left over. The clues never lie, and they’re enough to pin down every pairing without a single guess. The generator that built this puzzle rejected every clue set that needed trial and error.

item.title: Curtain Call at the Gaslight Theatre: A Murder Mystery Logic Grid
item.description:
Clue seven puts Mr. Bramwell and Mrs. Penrose on the bottom two floors of the dressing-room tower, one each, no telling which. Clue one says Bramwell didn’t dress on the first floor. You draw your first ● with some satisfaction. Then clue four turns that floor into an entrance cue, and suddenly a second block of the grid starts filling in too.

That chain reaction is what this case is about. There are two ordered categories here, acts and floors, and the clues keep passing information between them. Every actor had exactly one prop, one first entrance and one dressing-room floor. Eight clues, no guessing, and somewhere in the grid is the person who poisoned the goblet.

item.title: The Last Sitting at Hollowmere: A Hard Murder Mystery Logic Grid
item.description:
You’ve already decided it’s the Reverend. The arsenic was in a prayer book, and only one sitter that night wore a dog collar. Then you look at the grid: five sitters, five keepsakes, five relatives, five arrival times, and a hundred and fifty empty squares. The clues haven’t said a word about the Reverend being guilty. A hunch, you’ll discover, is not evidence.

This is a five-by-five logic grid. It plays by the same rules as the smaller cases: each sitter brought exactly one keepsake, mourned exactly one relative and arrived at exactly one time. The jump in size is the hard part. Four of the ten clues are “one or the other” pairs, and none of them solves anything on its own. They only start to pay off once you read them against each other.

item.title: The Locked Room: An Easy Sherlock Holmes Cryptogram
item.description:
The door is locked from the inside. The window is shut. The chimney is too narrow for a cat. And yet there’s a body in the chair, and Holmes is lecturing Watson about something he’s apparently said many, many times before. You know the line. You’ve probably quoted it yourself. Now find it under a layer of scrambled letters.

Every letter in the quote has been swapped for a different one, and the swap holds for the whole puzzle. If M stands for E once, it stands for E everywhere. No letter ever stands for itself, and the most common letter in the quote is filled in for free.

item.title: The Inspector's Question: An Easy Sherlock Holmes Cryptogram
item.description: The inspector has had enough. He’s walked the moor, searched the stables and arrested a bookmaker, and here is Holmes, about to climb back on a train, being cryptic. So the inspector asks him straight out whether there’s anything he ought to know. Holmes answers in one line, the inspector objects, and Holmes gets the last word. It’s four lines of dialogue, and one of the most quoted exchanges in detective fiction.

item.title: The Detective's Maxim: A Victorian Cryptogram
item.description:
You spot a two-letter word that starts with the free T. It has to be TO. You fill in the O, and suddenly an eight-letter word reads T _ _ O _ _ _ _ and your brain refuses to let it go. Five minutes later you’re muttering at a 135-year-old sentence about evidence. That’s the cryptogram effect: one right guess pays for itself everywhere the letter appears.

Every letter in the quote below has been swapped for a different letter, and the swap holds for the whole puzzle. If K means E once, it means E every time. No letter ever stands for itself. You get one letter free.

item.title: A Day in the Armchair: A Sherlock Holmes Cryptogram
item.description:
Watson comes home from his club after a wet day, and Holmes tells him exactly where he’s been. Watson concedes it’s “rather obvious”. Holmes, who has been sitting in the same armchair since breakfast surrounded by tobacco smoke, uses the moment to say something about how blind everybody else is. It’s one sentence. Holmes would like you to notice it.

This cipher is shorter than the easy ones, and short quotes are harder. There’s less text to compare, and fewer repeats to lean on. Every letter is swapped for a different one, the swap holds throughout, and one letter is given to you free. Make it work for its keep.

item.title: The Prefect's Problem: An Edgar Allan Poe Cryptogram
item.description:
The Prefect of the Paris police has taken a minister’s apartment apart. He’s probed the cushions with needles, checked the rungs of every chair and examined the floor with a microscope. Three months in, he drops into a chair in Dupin’s darkened library and admits the case is simple, and he’s still beaten. Dupin, smoking in the dark, offers one quiet suggestion. The Prefect laughs at him.

Poe created his detective more than forty years before Holmes, and he knew his ciphers too: “The Gold-Bug” turns on one. This quote is a single sentence. Every letter is swapped for a different one, the swap holds throughout, and one letter is given away.

item.title: Poirot's Rule: A Hard Agatha Christie Cryptogram
item.description:
Captain Hastings has spotted something odd, and he’s decided it doesn’t matter. He says so out loud, to Poirot, which is a mistake. A groan comes from the little Belgian, followed by two short sentences. Every Christie fan has met the idea behind them, even if they couldn’t quote the words.

This is the hard one: no free letter. Every letter is swapped for a different one, the swap holds throughout, and no letter stands for itself. You start with nothing but the shapes of the words, and the shapes turn out to be enough.

item.title: Detective Clues: A Murder Mystery Connections Puzzle
item.description:
You see SCARLET, MUSTARD, PLUM and BLUE, and you’re already reaching for the Submit button. Four colours, done. Except PEACOCK is sitting two tiles over, smirking. Now you have five candidates for four slots, one mistake on the board, and a creeping suspicion that this puzzle was written by someone who enjoys watching you squirm. It was.

The rules are short. Sixteen words hide four groups of four. Pick four you think belong together and submit. Find all four groups before you make four mistakes.

item.title: The Blackwood Estate: A Victorian Murder Escape
item.description:
The front door booms shut behind you and a bolt slides home on the far side. You didn’t hear anyone follow you up the drive. Somewhere down the hall is a dead man, a locked desk and three people who all have a very good reason to be somewhere else. The coachman is clear about it: nobody leaves until someone is named.

This is a narrative escape game, a little like a choose-your-own-adventure book that fights back. You read, you choose where to go, and when you hit a lock you have to work out the combination from what you’ve seen. Everything you need is somewhere in the house.
